video_title: What Ukraine Hath Wrought: Lessons for War, If We're Listening
gist: War on the Rocks panel (Ryan Evans with Michael Kofman, Dara Massicot and Amos Fox) argues the real lessons of nearly four years of war in Ukraine are not 'drones and AI' but force-structure reorganization, the enduring role of mass, attrition and terrain control, and the limits of precision and air power — lessons they say the US failed to apply before its war with Iran (Operation Epic Fury), leaving Middle East and UK bases exposed to drones.

themes.theme: Drone warfare is a force-structure and manpower problem, not a procurement problem

insights.claim: Panelists argue that Ukraine's real lesson is not 'drones and AI' but a fundamental reorganization of core war-fighting functions: embedding drone support and ISR in units, changing billets, and building a high-low mix, which US forces are largely not discussing.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Defense spend that buys drones without org/manning changes will underdeliver; watch for unit restructuring and billet changes as the real adoption signal.
insights.quote: it's just a really fundamental reorganization of core war fighting functions that need to happen

insights.claim: Drone warfare at scale is very manpower intensive: Russia and Ukraine did not simply buy drones but strategically reallocated manpower from maneuver formations, plus logistics and organizational capacity, into new support/fire/ISR formations that later also took on air defense.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Drone adoption implies demand for training, C2, logistics and enabling tech (networks, sensors), not just airframes; vendors of enabling layers benefit.
insights.quote: at least right now drone warfare is very manpower intensive

insights.claim: Drones work as a huge force multiplier to traditional land-warfare challenges — extensive offensive and defensive mining, artillery that prevents force concentration, and prepared defenses — so a force of only drones would fail; infantry, armor and artillery remain necessary.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Expect continued demand for artillery, mines and conventional land systems alongside drones rather than substitution.
insights.quote: you cannot have just a force of drones

insights.claim: Drones have proven to be one of the principal counters to drones in this war, with drone-on-drone fights resembling World War I aerial battles using interception, nets and guns.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Counter-UAS via interceptor drones is a growth niche; counter-drone and drone markets are coupled.
insights.quote: drones have proven at least in this war to be one of the principal counters to drones

themes.theme: Precision denies terrain but cannot control it — mass and attrition still matter

insights.claim: Amos Fox's 'precision paradox': precision solves problems but creates many more, driving positional warfare, and the West has replaced campaign planning with kill chains, kill webs and targeting.
insights.speaker: Amos Fox
insights.so_what: Doctrine fixated on strike packages may underinvest in sustained campaign capacity (munitions depth, ground forces).
insights.quote: we've replaced the idea of campaigns with kill chains and kill webs and targeting

insights.claim: Mass precision lets Ukraine hold terrain on the defense with an incredibly low density of forces, compensating for manpower shortfalls, but it only denies terrain to the enemy; taking and controlling terrain still requires boots on the ground and offensive operations.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Drone-heavy defense can stabilize fronts but not reverse territorial losses — relevant to war-duration and ceasefire-line expectations.
insights.quote: It allows you to deny control to your opponent. You still need boots on the ground.

insights.claim: Russia has physical mass and Ukraine does not; Russia's ability to hold terrain is the key obstacle preventing Ukraine from converting military operations into political outcomes.
insights.speaker: Amos Fox
insights.so_what: Supports a base case of a grinding, attritional war where Ukraine's manpower is the binding constraint.
insights.quote: Russia has the mass. Ukraine does not have the mass

insights.claim: Attrition is unavoidable: reliance on precision strike pushes adversaries underground, into urban terrain and dispersal, which forces the striker into attritional ground fighting whether it wants it or not; forces must be built and resourced at scale for that.
insights.speaker: Amos Fox
insights.so_what: Favors sustained production capacity (munitions, vehicles, replacement manpower) over exquisite low-volume systems.
insights.quote: It matters how you're going to have to fight.

insights.claim: Fox argues the US obsession with 'restoring maneuver' is misplaced: once forces converge, war becomes positional and attritional, and land forces on a transparent battlefield are like 'an M&M without a hard candy shell' — the priority is restoring protected mobility.
insights.speaker: Amos Fox
insights.so_what: Protection/survivability tech for land forces (active protection, counter-drone, signature management) is the unsolved need.
insights.quote: land forces essentially are operating like an Eminem without a hard candy shell

insights.claim: Russia over-optimized for small-scale infantry assaults and infiltration, an approach that became increasingly combat-inefficient, and failed to invest in restoring force quality, which will take it a while to recover from.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Russian offensive efficiency may remain low; watch for force-quality reconstitution as a signal of renewed offensive capacity.

themes.theme: Beware porting late-war lessons to the opening of the next war

insights.claim: Drones were not a defining element during the first year and a half of the Ukraine war; they began as artillery spotters, FPV drones emerged in early 2023, and drones only began to shut down mobility around August–September 2023.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Opening phases of future wars (e.g., US vs China) may look very different from the current positional phase; don't extrapolate linearly.
insights.quote: They begin to shut down mobility around August September of 2023.

insights.claim: Kofman warns that militaries tend to assume the opening phase of the next war will look like the last phase of the last war, which is probably wrong; context (e.g., US vs China in the Pacific) and war phasing differ, and some technologies such as the TB2 in Nagorno-Karabakh prove irrelevant in the next conflict.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Treat 'proven in Ukraine' marketing with caution when sizing defense-tech TAM for Pacific scenarios.
insights.quote: I think the opening phase of the next war will look like the last phase of the last war I saw and that's probably not going to be it.

themes.theme: Air power and base defense: gaps exposed in the Iran war

insights.claim: Panelists say the US failed to apply Ukraine's lessons before Operation Epic Fury against Iran: commercial imagery showed squadrons of high-value aircraft stacked on Middle East bases with air defenses but basically no drone defense, no dispersal and no hardened C2, and the US was lucky Iran did not strike then.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Base hardening, dispersal and counter-UAS for US overseas bases is an under-funded need now being prioritized.
insights.quote: we had no hardened C2

insights.claim: The Air Force is only now saying it needs to prioritize base force protection, four years after Russia and Ukraine began hardening bases with underground structures, dispersal, drone nets and decoys.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Expect rising budgets for hardened shelters, drone nets, decoys and base counter-drone systems.
insights.quote: the Air Force says, okay, like we need to prioritize base force protection four years later

insights.claim: A drone threat against RAF Fairford in the UK reportedly forced US bombers to be lofted and moved because of an inability to detect drones, even though such capability exists in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Drone detection at allied air bases is an immediate procurement gap; watch for counter-UAS contracts at European bases.
insights.quote: we had to loft all the bombers and get them out of there because we didn't have the ability to detect drones

insights.claim: The Iran war exposed US bases as vulnerable to asymmetric capabilities, forcing a distant logistics pathway at some cost to aircraft carriers, and panelists say the US has not been open about how hard it was hit in the Middle East.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Power-projection risk and base vulnerability may drive spending on hardening, dispersal and long-range logistics.
insights.quote: we haven't talked about how hard we got hit

insights.claim: Air superiority may deliver localized control yet fail to stop an adversary with scaled mass-precision fire control over ground forces, and air power is not able to conduct air defense against these systems at scale without substantial adaptation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Ground-based point defense and SHORAD for maneuver forces is under-built because of assumed air superiority — a likely growth area.

insights.claim: Russia is procuring over 120,000 large one-way attack drones this year, which air power alone cannot answer.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Scale of Shahed/Geran-class threats implies huge demand for low-cost interceptors and layered air defense in Europe.
insights.quote: Russia is procuring over 120,000 large oneway attack drones this year

themes.theme: Institutional learning failures and who is learning faster

insights.claim: The US lacks embedded forward observers in Ukraine — being in Kyiv is not being a forward observer — and relies on filtered, remote knowledge plus a small group of freelance analysts, leading it to start from technology rather than force-employment requirements.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Expect US adaptation to lag; firms with direct battlefield feedback loops (e.g., Ukrainian-tested vendors) have an edge.
insights.quote: being in Kev is not being a forward observer

insights.claim: North Korea is making big moves reorganizing its forces around drone warfare based on direct experience in Russia, and China may draw smarter lessons for its contingencies than the US, which dismisses Ukraine as geographically irrelevant despite long-range systems like the Geran.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Adversary adaptation raises threat baselines in Korea and Taiwan scenarios, supporting regional defense spending.

insights.claim: Fox argues many are learning bad lessons through a 'task completion bias' — counting drone strikes and kills without asking whether they advance political objectives — citing a British general who said he doesn't think about strategy.
insights.speaker: Amos Fox
insights.so_what: Strike-count metrics are poor indicators of war outcomes; discount headline kill statistics.
insights.quote: We're getting caught up in a task completion bias

themes.theme: Stand-in forces, allies and legacy armor

insights.claim: Lessons differ by force: for the US as an expeditionary power fighting 'away games,' the challenge is logistics to reach allies; for front-line states like Estonia or Taiwan, which must serve as the stand-in force, survival of that force is the core problem.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: Front-line states will prioritize survivability, drones and attritable systems; US prioritizes logistics and power projection — different procurement mixes.

insights.claim: Western and Russian main battle tanks — US, British, German, Russian — are essentially 1980s platforms with upgrades; armor optimization dates to the Cold War and hasn't had a generational revolution from 1985 to 2025.
insights.speaker: Michael Kofman (captioned 'Mike Kaufman')
insights.so_what: A next-generation armor/protection cycle looks overdue; watch for new-generation vehicle programs.
insights.quote: we're actually all pretty much driving tanks from 1980s

insights.claim: Ukraine-style infantry suppression means soldiers sit isolated in positions for long periods with telemedicine and drone-delivered supply and no helicopter casualty evacuation, implying infantry should be trained almost like Rangers — a major shift from the GWOT 'golden hour' assumption.
insights.speaker: Dara Massicot (captioned 'Dar Masico')
insights.so_what: Demand for telemedicine, drone-based resupply and self-aid medical kits for dispersed forces.
insights.quote: infantry should start to be trained almost like rangers
